title: CSS Box Model
subtitle: Understand the space around every HTML element
description: Learn how content, padding, borders, and margins work together to control the size, spacing, and layout of web pages.

blocks.title: PAGE 1: Understanding the CSS Box Model
blocks.text:
Every HTML element displayed on a web page can be understood as a rectangular box. A heading, paragraph, button, image container, and card all occupy space. CSS uses the box model to determine how that space is measured and how elements sit beside or away from one another.

The box model has four main parts, from the inside outward:

1. Content: The actual text, image, or other content inside the element.
2. Padding: The space between the content and its border.
3. Border: The line surrounding the content and padding.
4. Margin: The space outside the border that separates the element from other elements.

Imagine a course card. The course title is the content. The space around the title inside the card is padding. The outline around the card is its border. The gap between that card and another card is margin.

These four parts have different jobs. Padding creates internal breathing room, while margin creates external separation. A border visually separates the element from its surroundings. Understanding this difference helps you build clean interfaces instead of trying random spacing values.

blocks.question: You are designing a course card. The text is too close to the card's border, but you want to keep the card's outside position unchanged. Which property should you adjust first?
blocks.explanation: Padding creates space between an element's content and its border. Increasing it gives the text more internal breathing room. Margin creates space outside the border.
blocks.hint: Choose the property that controls space inside the border.

blocks.title: Understanding Sample Code 1
blocks.text:
Look carefully at the .course-box rule.

The width: 250px declaration sets the width of the content area by default. The padding: 20px declaration adds 20 pixels to the left and right inside the box. The border adds another 3 pixels on each side. The margin: 20px declaration adds space outside the border.

With the default box-sizing: content-box, the total horizontal width is:

250px content + 40px padding + 6px border = 296px.

The left and right margins add another 40 pixels to the space the element occupies in the surrounding layout, making its total horizontal footprint 336 pixels when those margins are included.

This distinction is important. If you set width to 250 pixels, the complete visible box will be wider than 250 pixels when padding and borders are added. This surprises many developers when they first create layouts.

blocks.question: An element has width: 250px, padding: 20px, and border: 3px solid blue. It uses the default box-sizing: content-box. What is the element's total visible width, excluding margins?
blocks.explanation: The visible width is 250px content + 40px horizontal padding + 6px horizontal border = 296px. The margins are excluded from this calculation.
blocks.hint: Remember to count both left and right padding and both borders.

blocks.title: PAGE 2: Padding and Internal Spacing
blocks.text:
Padding controls the space inside an element, between its content and its border. It is especially useful for buttons, cards, navigation links, input fields, and notification panels.

CSS lets you set padding on all four sides or control individual sides. For example, padding: 16px gives all four sides 16 pixels of padding. padding: 10px 20px gives 10 pixels to the top and bottom and 20 pixels to the left and right. padding: 5px 10px 15px 20px sets top, right, bottom, and left in that order.

You can also use padding-top, padding-right, padding-bottom, and padding-left when only one side needs adjustment.

Padding improves readability because text does not sit directly against the edges of a box. However, excessive padding can make cards too large, push important content down the page, or make a mobile layout feel crowded. Choose spacing deliberately and test the result on a small screen.

blocks.title: Reading the Padding Example
blocks.text:
Both boxes contain text and have borders. The difference is the padding value. The first box uses 5px, so the text stays relatively close to its border. The second uses 20px, so the text has more space around it.

Notice that margin-bottom: 12px is used on the first box. This creates a gap outside the blue box, separating it from the green box. It does not create space between the text and the blue border.

When debugging a layout, ask yourself two separate questions: Is the content too close to its own border, or is the entire element too close to another element? The first problem usually calls for padding. The second may call for margin or a layout gap.

blocks.question: A button's label is comfortable to read, but the button is too close to the next button. Which change is most directly aimed at creating space between the two buttons?
options: Add suitable margin or use a gap on their layout container
blocks.explanation: Margin or a layout container's gap can separate neighboring elements. Padding changes the internal space inside each button instead.
blocks.hint: The problem is the space between separate elements, not inside a button.

blocks.title: PAGE 3: Margins, Borders, and Element Separation
blocks.text:
Margin is the space outside an element's border. It helps separate cards, headings, paragraphs, images, and other components. You can set margin on all sides or use margin-top, margin-right, margin-bottom, and margin-left.

For example, margin-bottom: 24px creates 24 pixels of space below an element. margin: 10px 20px sets 10 pixels for the top and bottom and 20 pixels for the left and right.

A border sits between padding and margin. It can be styled with width, line style, and color. For example, border: 2px solid #2563eb creates a two-pixel solid blue outline. A border can also be dashed or dotted. The border-radius property rounds corners, but it does not replace the border's width or style.

One detail to understand is that vertical margins between some normal block elements can collapse. This means the resulting gap may be the larger of the adjoining margins rather than their sum. For example, two adjoining vertical margins of 20px and 30px may produce a 30px gap, not 50px. This behavior depends on the layout context, so do not assume every pair of margins simply adds together.

blocks.title: Why the Cards Look Organized
blocks.text:
The .card class is reused on both article elements. Each card gets padding: 16px, which keeps its text away from the border. The border declaration draws the outline, and border-radius rounds its corners. margin-bottom: 20px creates separation below each card.

The rule .card h2 selects an h2 heading inside an element with the card class. Setting margin-top: 0 removes the heading's default top margin in that context. This can help the content align more neatly with the top padding of the card.

Do not confuse margin with padding. If you increase a card's margin, you move it away from surrounding elements. If you increase its padding, you give the content more room inside the card. A border helps you see the boundary between those areas.

blocks.question: You want more distance between two course cards, but the text inside each card already has enough space. Which is the best first adjustment?
options: Increase the cards' margin-bottom or the container's gap
Add more text to each card
blocks.explanation: Margin or a parent layout's gap separates neighboring cards without changing the internal spacing around their text.
blocks.hint: Think about the space outside each card.

blocks.question: Which CSS declaration correctly creates a visible 2-pixel dotted green border?
blocks.explanation: The border shorthand accepts a width, a style, and a color. The declaration border: 2px dotted green correctly supplies all three.
blocks.hint: Include the width, the dotted style, and the color in the border shorthand.

blocks.title: PAGE 4: Total Width, box-sizing, and Real-World Layouts
blocks.text:
The box model becomes especially important when building responsive layouts. A card may appear wider than expected because its declared width can exclude padding and borders.

With box-sizing: content-box, the width property sets the content width. The final visible width adds left and right padding and borders. With box-sizing: border-box, the declared width includes the content, padding, and border. This often makes layout sizing easier to predict.

For example, if an element has width: 300px, padding: 20px, and a 2px border on each side, content-box produces a visible width of 344px: 300 + 40 + 4. Under border-box, the visible width stays 300px, and the content area becomes narrower to make room for the padding and borders.

Many developers use the universal selector to apply box-sizing: border-box to all elements. This is a common layout convention, not a requirement of CSS. You should understand which sizing model your page uses before calculating widths.

blocks.title: Understanding the Final Example

blocks.question: A panel must remain exactly 300px wide, including 20px padding on both sides and a 2px border on both sides. Which sizing choice makes this requirement easiest to express?
blocks.explanation: With box-sizing: border-box, the declared 300px width includes the content, padding, and borders. The content area adjusts to fit inside that total.
blocks.hint: Choose the sizing model that includes padding and borders in the declared width.

blocks.title: Final Practical Challenge
blocks.text:
Build a responsive course card using everything from this lesson. Give the card a maximum width, internal padding, a visible border, rounded corners, and margin or layout gap to separate it from nearby content. Apply box-sizing: border-box so its declared width includes its padding and border.

Test your card at a narrow phone width and a wider screen. Check that text does not touch the border, cards do not overlap, and the layout does not create unwanted horizontal scrolling.

Before finishing, explain the difference between content, padding, border, and margin in your own words. Then calculate the visible width of an element with width: 200px, padding: 10px on each side, and a 1px border on each side under content-box sizing. If you can explain the calculation and choose the correct spacing property for a layout problem, you are ready to continue.

blocks.question: A box uses width: 200px, padding: 10px on all sides, and border: 1px solid black. With box-sizing: content-box, what is its visible width excluding margins?
blocks.explanation: The total visible width is 200px content + 20px horizontal padding + 2px horizontal border = 222px. Margins are not included.
blocks.hint: Add the content width, both horizontal padding values, and both border widths.

blocks.question: Your page develops unwanted horizontal scrolling after you add padding and borders to a fixed-width card. What is the most useful first step?
options: Delete every border on the page
Inspect the card's sizing model and calculate its content, padding, and border widths
Add more margin to the card
blocks.explanation: Inspecting the sizing model and the total width helps identify whether padding and borders are making the card wider than its available space. Then choose an appropriate sizing or responsive layout fix.
blocks.hint: Find the cause of the extra width before changing unrelated styles.
